# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

== explorations/reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md:5-15

## 1. Coherence

The design is one rule: a numeral converts where it stands, into the declared type, else into the machine default. Six cases get two answers or none; each has a repair.

- Undefined: what "fixes a type". Point 1 lists `Any`; the fork review adds `Object`, `Number` and an unbounded `T` (§1.1); the prototype defaulted at all (probe §1, step 2). Repair: a place fixes a type when its declared type declares a coercion from the numeral type (the eight number types; a program's type by point 4) or is a numeral type; every other type, and no type, takes the default. Then `f(3)` at `Number` is a `ZZ32`, and a tuple at `Any` defaults element by element.
- Two answers: "by its value" where the value is unknown. Row 946 shows it: a variable of numeral type reads `ZZ32` whatever its value. Inside `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, `t = x` is such an expression; so is a `nat` used as a value, whose value a template does not know (probe §8). Repair: the default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of numeral type; a `nat` used as a value has the type the Draft gives, `NN32` (`trait-parameters.tex:84-86`), or `ZZ32` (P-40), chosen once.
- Two answers: the fold against the fields. Point 4 reads the written numeral's four numbers; point 5 folds `7/2`, `-3` and `0.1 + 0.2` into "one numeral", which has no written form: the prototype made `1/3` a radix-3 numeral (probe §1, step 3), and a negative result has no `nat v`. Repair: the fold yields a constant with a sign, as the Draft's `IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]` has one (`constant.tex:49-52`): an integer constant defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient to `QQ`, one with a radix point to `RR64`; a program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only.
- Two answers: a static argument that several numerals fix. `<|3000000000, 0.5|>` is a `List[\RR64\]` if each numeral converts exactly into one instantiation, refused if each defaults first (`ZZ64` into `RR64` is written, P-74); an `if` join likewise. Repair: the narrowest default holding every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each converting into it exactly: the tie rule's form (`inference.tex:313-317`).
- Two answers: a program's type with no coercion from the numeral type. The prototype chained default and own coercion (probe §10, decision 3); the Draft says coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:407-408`). Repair: refuse, or name the chain as the one exception.
- Undefined: "once per class, at load" as a semantics. For a reference object two evaluations of `c: CC64 = 3` become one object, which `SEQV` sees (`objects.tex:51-53`), and a raising coercion fails at load. Repair: a numeral at a program's type denotes one object, as a string literal does (P-171), or hoist value types only.
- One answer, for the record: `-3` is `-` on a numeral (`lexical-structure.tex:1053-1080`); folded, `-2147483648` fits `ZZ32` and `u: NN32 = -3` is refused. `x = 3` then `x` at `ZZ64` converts (P-74), at `NN32` is refused (fork §6.1), point 1's rule. `pi: RadixPointNumeral` (`Constants.fsi:16-17`) is refused by the fifth default and becomes `RR64`. Two numeral values inside a body: by P-168 value objects compare field by field, so `2.5` and `2.50` differ there, as the Draft's types differ; elsewhere both default and are `SEQV`.

# Rung N, rung-numeral-types: the numeral types NaturalNumeral and RadixPointNumeral below Numeral, each number type's coercions and = pairs, the 24 glue bindings gone, and walk's numerals converted where they stand

- problem: walk keeps a float numeral at `RR64` a `FloatLiteral` (row 943, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:635`), `QQ` takes no float numeral (row 944, `:636`), `NN32`, `NN64` and `RR32` refuse numerals (row 454, `:610`), `RR64` refuses 3000000000 (row 443, `:609`), `u + 1` at `NN32` is a `ZZ64` (row 484, `:156`), `round(2.5_10)` throws (row 361, `:602`), and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic answers a `ZZ32` (row 578, `:620`)
- spec: `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148` (numerals have their own types, which libraries convert by coercions) and `:83-129` (the four numbers); `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:145-153`
- precedent: `value object Ratio(num: ZZ, den: ZZ) extends { QQ }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:648` at the base), the prototype's library step (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.patch:1-400`), and `Types.CHARACTER`'s switch by library (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java:78-91` at the base)
- deviation: walk converts a numeral into the eight number types through the library's own coercion, called once per site and type, not by a Java conversion per type (fork N7) (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Coercions.java:88-115`); `RR32`'s rounding binding sits in `FortressBuiltin`, beside `RR32`, and `RR64`'s and the numerals' in `FortressLibrary` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:208-210`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:668-670`); `strToFloat` gains a `ZZ32` base, a line beyond the declarations the brief names (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4839-4840`)
- historical: `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, `Library/Constants.fsi`, `Library/Constants.fss`, `Library/ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`, `compiler/Types.java`, `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`, `nativeHelpers/simpleDoubleArith.java`, `interpreter/env/LazilyEvaluatedCell.java`, `interpreter/evaluator/{BaseEnv,Evaluator,EvaluatorBase,Init,LHSEvaluator}.java`, `interpreter/evaluator/values/{FBigNum,FFloat,FInt,FLong,FOrdinaryObject,FunctionClosure,GenericFunctionOrConstructor,MethodClosure,NonPrimitive,OverloadedFunction,OverloadedMethod}.java` (under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`), and the team's tests `ProjectFortress/tests/NumberPrintTest.fss`, `sequivTest.fss`, `XXXextendIntLiteral.fss`, `XXXextendFloatLiteral.fss`

Commits on `wip/rung-numeral-types`: `f7b46ce742` (the tests, before any edit), `9e259096a9` (the library, walk and the checker), `d541ae9682` (the test changes and walk's inference hook), `e3adeedb64` (`strToFloat`'s base and the XXX test of an undefined `typecase` arm). Every stage and suite named below ran on the commit it names.

## What changed and why

**The library.** `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:454-494` and `.fss:668-721` declare, beside `Ratio`, `trait Numeral extends Number comprises { NaturalNumeral, RadixPointNumeral }` with the four getters abstract (`digits`, `fractionDigits` and `radix` at `ZZ32`, `digitValue` at `ZZ`), and the value objects `NaturalNumeral(digits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ)`, whose `fractionDigits` is 0, and `RadixPointNumeral(digits: ZZ32, fractionDigits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ)`. Each has `asString`, the numeral as the Working Draft writes one (its digits in its radix, at least `digits` of them, upper case, the radix point after `digits - fractionDigits` of them, `_r` where the radix is not ten), `asFloat(self): RR64` by one rounding, and its reversed `=` pairs: `NaturalNumeral` at the eight number types, `RadixPointNumeral` at `RR64`, `QQ` and `RR32`, each `do c: T = self; (c = b) end` as the library writes its pairs (`.fss:418` at the base). The number types' coercions, renamed or new, each with its pair:

| type | coercions from the numeral types, and their bodies | pair |
|---|---|---|
| `RR64` | `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) = asFloat(x)`, `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = asFloat(x)` (`.fss:389-390`) | both (`.fss:419-420`) |
| `QQ` | `Ratio(x.digitValue, 1)`; `x.digitValue / r^(x.fractionDigits)` for `r: ZZ = big(x.radix)`, reduced by `ZZ`'s `/` (`.fss:565-569`) | both (`.fss:588-589`) |
| `AnyIntegral` | `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by the value, which is never negative (`.fss:723-728`) | none, as at the base |
| `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64`, `ZZ` | `x.digitValue.asZZ32`, `.asZZ64`, `.asNN64`, `x.digitValue` (`.fss:829`, `:935`, `:1045`, `:1155`) | `NaturalNumeral` (`:845`, `:956`, `:1064`, `:1175`) |
| `NN32` | `x.digitValue.asNN32` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:430`) | `NaturalNumeral` (`:453`) |
| `RR32` | `numeralRR32(x.digitValue, x.radix, 0)` and `numeralRR32(x.digitValue, x.radix, x.fractionDigits)` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:214-215`) | both, new (`:258-259`) |

`RR64` comprises `{ Float }` (`.fsi:294`); `Float`'s `asFloat(self): RR64` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:82`); the `^` over the numeral in `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64`, `ZZ` and `NN32` renamed, its body `self^(b.digitValue.asZZ32)`; `pi` and `e` at `RR64` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`, `.fss:15-16`); `ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss:40` chooses `theType[\ZZ32\]()` where it chose `IntLiteral`, and the arm `theType[\IntLiteral\]() => Just[\AnyGen\](genZZ32)` (`:157` at the base), which repeated the `ZZ32` arm above it, is dropped. `value object IntLiteral` and `value object FloatLiteral` leave `FortressBuiltin.fsi` and `.fss` with their 24 glue bindings; no line of the one library names either now. The glue classes `interpreter/glue/prim/IntLiteral.java` and `FloatLiteral.java`, and walk's `FIntLiteral` and `FFloatLiteral`, stay in the tree, unused (fork N11).

**The helper pair** (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleDoubleArith.java:264-307`): `public static double numeralToDouble(BigInteger v, int r, int m)` and `public static float numeralToFloat(BigInteger v, int r, int m)`, the value `v / r^m` rounded once to the nearest double or float, ties to even, subnormals included, by an integer quotient at the format's last significand bit and its remainder; two private helpers (`lsbExponent`, `roundedQuotient`) whose types all map to Fortress, as the wrapper generator needs. The bindings: `private numeralRR64(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR64` in `FortressLibrary.fss:668-670`, which both numerals' `asFloat` call, and `private numeralRR32(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR32` in `FortressBuiltin.fss:208-210`, which `RR32`'s coercions call; walk carries `ZZ` in `BigInteger`, `ZZ32` in `int`, `RR64` in `double` and `RR32` in `float` (F-299). Walk's default for a radix-point numeral calls `numeralToDouble` in Java (`Numerals.java`), so the default and `RR64`'s coercion round alike.

**Walk's numerals** (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`, new). `Evaluator.forIntLiteralExpr` and `forFloatLiteralExpr` (`Evaluator.java:1632`, `:1636`) return the value of the numeral's site, made once: its default, a subclass of `FInt`, `FLong`, `FBigNum` or `FFloat` (their constructors opened to the package) that carries a `Site` with the four numbers. The digits as written come from the numeral's text, since the node keeps the value and not the trailing zeros (`3.14150` has `digitValue` 314150, `fractionDigits` 5). The places:

- a typed binding, a field and an assignment (`LHSEvaluator.java:115`, `:220-230`, `BaseEnv.java:332`, `LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:69`), a parameter (`NonPrimitive.java:247`, `:272`), and a declared return type (`FunctionClosure.java:212-221`, `MethodClosure.java:85-89`, `Numerals.atReturn`): where the default does not fit the type, `Coercions.coerce` makes a numeral the numeral object at a numeral type, else converts it through the place type's coercion whose parameter type is the narrowest holding the numeral type, with no chain through the default (`Coercions.java:59`, `:88-115`, `:268`); the result is kept for the site and type (`Numerals.converted`), so a site gives one object of a reference type; a store keeps the default alone (`Numerals.plain`, deep for tuples);
- an integer numeral outside an integer type's range is not converted, so the place refuses it as walk refused one at a binding before: 'Type mismatch binding 3000000000' (`Numerals.inRange`);
- dispatch (`OverloadedFunction.java:2278-2342`, `:2712`): a declaration fits a numeral as it is where its parameter is the numeral's own type or admits its default; of those, the one that the defaults alone fit, unless the own-type fit's domain lies strictly below it; with no fit, the coercion attempt, each numeral converting only from its own type; and a tie among those, an ambiguous coercion, reads each numeral at its default; a functional method chosen at a numeral's own type receives the numeral object before walk finds the method on it (`Coercions.withNumeralObjects`). The three dispatch caches key a numeral apart from a value of its default type (`Numerals.keys`; `OverloadedFunction.java:99`, `OverloadedMethod.java:29`, `GenericFunctionOrConstructor.java:24`);
- the head of `EvaluatorBase.inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction` (`EvaluatorBase.java:90`): the inference reads each numeral at its default, and where the numerals at one type parameter's positions include a radix point, one beyond `ZZ32` by a `ZZ32` stand-in, so that walk's promotion gives `RR64`; the call's numerals then convert at the instance;
- `SEQV` (`FOrdinaryObject.java:48-49`): two numeral objects compare by `digitValue / radix^fractionDigits`, reduced, across both numeral types;
- `Init.java:46` empties the sites between runs.

**The checker.** `Types.INT_LITERAL` and `FLOAT_LITERAL` are no longer final and switch with the libraries, as `CHARACTER` does: the prelude's `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` under the compiler's, `FortressLibrary`'s `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` under the one library (`Types.java:61-62`, `:75-95`). `Functionals.isNumeral` counts a numeral with a radix point, and `numeralReading` reads one as `RR64` (`Functionals.scala:418-444`), the prototype's tie rule, written inside the two functions and with no new function, since rung C adds functions near them.

**`strToFloat`** (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4839-4840`): its `10^k` and `10^(|frac|)` became `ten^k` for `ten: ZZ32 = 10`. Without it the count stage found two errors there ("The stages").

## The runs

The failing run, on the base's code (my worktree before any edit, `b430f9f428`), at 01:40:41 and 01:41:05 UTC:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh $PWD/tmp/rung-numeral-types/h-base ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralTypesWalk.fss ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk.fss ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk.test ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralOutOfRangeWalk.fss ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralOutOfRangeWalk.test

    tmp/rung-numeral-types/h-base/tests/NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss:63:10-25:
        RadixPointNumeral is undefined.
     OK Saw expected refusal at load
    Tests run: 4,  Failures: 3,  Errors: 0

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh $PWD/tmp/rung-numeral-types/h-base ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralTypesWalk.fss
    FAIL: 1/2 = 0.5 through QQ's = with the float numeral
    Tests run: 1,  Failures: 1,  Errors: 0

The first of the two had `NumeralTypesWalk` stop on a name of mine (`big`, a library function); the second, after the rename, is its failing run. The final versions of the tests, the promoted ones among them, on the old code through the base build's harness, at 02:15:56 UTC:

    FORTRESS_HOME=/home/user/fortress-base29 /home/user/fortress-base29/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh $PWD/tmp/rung-numeral-types/old-harness $W/NumeralTypesWalk.fss $W/NumeralOwnTypeWalk.fss $W/NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk.fss $W/NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk.test $W/NumeralOutOfRangeWalk.fss $W/NumeralOutOfRangeWalk.test $W/NumeralBeyondZZ32AtRR64.fss $W/NumeralWithNN32.fss $W/RadixTenPointNumeral.fss $W/RoundNearTieNumeral.fss $W/XXXNumeralLeftOfRR32Walk.fss
    FAIL: J8/0:6 : ZZ64 =/= J8/0:6 : NN32; literals.tex, section "Literals", and conversions-coercions.tex, ...
    RHS expression type Long is not assignable to LHS type RR64
    Caused by: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "2.5_10"

## Decisions

1. **Walk's numeral is its default, a subclass of `FInt`, `FLong`, `FBigNum` or `FFloat` carrying the four numbers, one value per site, and every store keeps the default alone.** Ways not taken: the numeral object at every evaluation (fork N7's way not taken: every `i + 1` would dispatch by coercion); a reading of the literal node at each place, which dispatch cannot do, since it receives values. Evidence: `x + 1` dispatches as before (walk suite), `y = 0.1` then a `QQ` place sees the plain `RR64`.
2. **Into the eight number types walk converts through the library's own coercion from the numeral type, called with the numeral object and kept for the site and type, not by a Java conversion per type.** The way not taken: fork N7's 'in walk's Java, by the same conversion as the library's coercion'. Evidence: the conversion is the library's by construction, one code path for the eight and a program's type; a site pays once. The integer types' range is checked in Java first, so an out-of-range numeral is refused with walk's binding message ('Type mismatch binding 3000000000', `NumeralOutOfRangeWalk`) rather than the coercion's `IntegerOverflow`. No decision on record covers the way; I acted on the brief's intent, the same value.
3. **Dispatch: the own-type fit, the default compared, the coercion attempt from the own type only, and a tie read at the defaults only on an ambiguous coercion.** Ways not taken: retrying at the defaults whenever no declaration applies, which would chain a numeral through its default into a program's `coerce(x: ZZ32)` (C4 refuses it; `NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk`); preferring the own-type fit always, which runs `ZZ32`'s `=(self, b: NaturalNumeral)` for `x = 0` through a Fortress object where `=(ZZ32, ZZ32)` fits. Evidence: fork N6, P-49.
4. **The dispatch caches' key adds, for a numeral, the bottom type, its default's type and its numeral type.** Ways not taken: a second cache for numeral calls; no caching of them. Evidence: `u = 0` and `u = z` for a `ZZ32 z` choose different declarations at the same types.
5. **The inference hook reads numerals at their defaults and, beside a radix point, a numeral beyond `ZZ32` by a `ZZ32` stand-in.** The way not taken, my first: each numeral of the group as an `RR64` value, under which walk infers the object `Float` and the team's `commonSuper` failed. Evidence: `second(0.5, 3000000000)` is the `RR64` 3000000000.0, `commonSuper` passes.
6. **The return conversion in `FunctionClosure` and `MethodClosure`, at a declared return type only; elsewhere the default.** Walk checks no return type, so a numeral that does not convert there is its default. The way not taken: conversion at bindings and fields only (fork N7's).
7. **The helpers in `simpleDoubleArith`, over `(BigInteger v, int r, int m)`.** Ways not taken: a new class; `QQ`'s `asFloat`, which rounds up to three times (fork N5). `RR32`'s binding is in `FortressBuiltin` beside `RR32`, since a private function of `FortressLibrary` is not visible there; `RR64`'s in `FortressLibrary`.

Meaning: rows 943, 944, 454, 443, 484 and 361 close; walk's answers are the checker's where the checker converts.
4. **Walk's choice of a declaration reads a numeral argument as the checker does.** A declaration fits a numeral as it is where the parameter is the numeral's own type or admits its default; the one that the defaults alone fit wins unless the own-type fit is strictly below it; without a fit, the coercion attempt converts each numeral from its own type only (no chain through its default); a tie among the declarations so found reads each numeral at its default (`OverloadedFunction.bestMatchForNumerals`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:2295-2342`). Evidence: `1/2 = 0.5`, `0.5 = 1/2`, `u0 = 0`, `f0 = 0.0`, `1.0 s` RR64 in `NumeralTypesWalk.fss`; `ProjectFortress/tests/NumeralNoCoercionRefusedWalk.fss` (a type with only `coerce(x: ZZ32)` refuses 3: 'Type mismatch binding 3'). Meaning: P-49's rule holds under walk for numerals; the dispatch caches key a numeral apart from a value of its default type (`Numerals.keys`).
5. **A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default holding them all under walk.** Walk's promotion joins the defaults; a numeral beyond `ZZ32` beside a radix-point numeral is read by a `ZZ32` stand-in so that the join is `RR64`, and the call's numerals convert at the instance (`EvaluatorBase.java:90`, `Numerals.forInference`). Meaning: the hook gives walk the checker's instance for `f[\A\](x: A, y: A)` over numerals.
6. **Two numeral objects are strictly equivalent by their reduced values, across both numeral types.** `FOrdinaryObject.seqv` takes the two numeral types as its exception (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/FOrdinaryObject.java:48-49`). Evidence: the count stage on `e3adeedb64`, `#total 0`, `#locations 0`, `#crash none`; `ant testQuick` 86, 263 and 1475 tests, 0 failures. (`checker-count/run.sh`, `#total 2`, `#locations 1`, on `d541ae9682`). The checker's numeral tie rule needs the tied declarations to differ only at the numeral, and the exponent's declared types differ. Meaning: rung C's narrow step 5, which ranks the numeral's conversion into its default as no coercion, resolves such a call as it is on the merged tree; the line is the library's only such site.

## For FACTS

**Walk's numeral is its default, carrying the numeral's four numbers, and converts from them where its place fixes a type.** An integer numeral is a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, a radix-point numeral the `RR64` nearest its value, one value per site (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`); at a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter, a declared return type and a coercion it converts through the place type's coercion from `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, called with the numeral object, one result per site and type, and a store keeps its default alone; dispatch fits it as it is at its own type or its default, then by its own type's coercions only, and reads a tie at the default. #!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

(* A numeral takes its default where nothing fixes a type, and converts from its exact value where a declared number type fixes one. *)
component NumeralTypesWalk
export Executable

kind(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    ZZ32 => "ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => "ZZ64"
    NN32 => "NN32"
    NN64 => "NN64"
    ZZ => "ZZ"
    QQ => "QQ"
    RR64 => "RR64"
    RR32 => "RR32"
    else => "another type"
  end

atAny(v: Any): String = kind(v)
atNumber(v: Number): String = kind(v)
second[\T\](a: T, b: T): T = b

run(): () = do
    (* The defaults: literals.tex, section "Literals"; inference.tex, section "A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie". *)
    x = 3
    assert(kind(x), "ZZ32", "x = 3 is a ZZ32")
    z: ZZ32 = 3
    assert(x SEQV z, "x = 3 is SEQV a ZZ32 3")
    y = 0.5
    assert(kind(y), "RR64", "y = 0.5 is an RR64")
    w: RR64 = 0.5
    assert(y SEQV w, "y = 0.5 is SEQV an RR64 0.5")
    bigN = 3000000000
    assert(kind(bigN), "ZZ64", "bigN = 3000000000 is a ZZ64")
    assert(atAny(3), "ZZ32", "3 at Any is a ZZ32")
    assert(atAny(0.5), "RR64", "0.5 at Any is an RR64")
    assert(atNumber(3), "ZZ32", "3 at Number is a ZZ32")
    (* A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default holding them all. *)
    assert(kind(second(13.0, 5)), "RR64", "second(13.0, 5) is at RR64")
    assert(second(13.0, 5) SEQV 5.0, "second(13.0, 5) is the RR64 5.0")
    assert(kind(second(0.5, 3000000000)), "RR64", "second(0.5, 3000000000) is at RR64")
    assert(second(0.5, 3000000000) SEQV 3000000000.0, "second(0.5, 3000000000) is the RR64 3000000000.0")
    assert(kind(second(1, 3000000000)), "ZZ64", "second(1, 3000000000) is at ZZ64")
    assert(1/2 = 0.5, "1/2 = 0.5 through QQ's = with the float numeral")
    assert(0.5 = 1/2, "0.5 = 1/2 through the reversed =")
    b = 0.9
    assert(kind(1 - b), "RR64", "1 - b is an RR64")
    assert(kind(b^2), "RR64", "b^2 is an RR64")
    s: ZZ32 = 4
    assert(kind(1.0 s), "RR64", "1.0 s is an RR64")
    assert((1.0 s) SEQV w 8, "1.0 s is the RR64 4.0")

    (* The typed places: the numeral converts from its exact value. *)
    q: QQ = 0.1
    assert(numerator(q), 1, "q: QQ = 0.1 has numerator 1")
    assert(denominator(q), 10, "q: QQ = 0.1 has denominator 10")
    one: RR64 = w + w
    ten: RR64 = one + one + one + one + one + one + one + one + one + one
    r: RR64 = 0.1
    assert(r SEQV (one / ten), "r: RR64 = 0.1 is SEQV a computed RR64 0.1")
    t: RR64 = 0.77425264282026984
    assert(t.asString, "0.7742526428202698", "the numeral at RR64 rounds once")
    n: NN32 = 5
    assert(n, unsigned(5), "n: NN32 = 5")
    assert(kind(n), "NN32", "n: NN32 = 5 is an NN32")
    m: NN64 = 5
    assert(kind(m), "NN64", "m: NN64 = 5 is an NN64")
    r32: RR32 = 0.1
    assert(kind(r32), "RR32", "r32: RR32 = 0.1 is an RR32")
    assert(asFloat(r32) SEQV asFloat(narrow(one / ten)), "r32: RR32 = 0.1 is the float nearest 0.1")
    near: RR32 = 1.0000000596046447763
    assert(asFloat(near) SEQV 1.0000001192092896, "a numeral just above a float midpoint rounds once, up, at RR32")
    wide: RR64 = 3000000000
    assert(wide SEQV 3000000000.0, "s: RR64 = 3000000000 holds the float 3000000000.0")
    u: NN32 = 5
    assert(kind(u + 1), "NN32", "u + 1 for an NN32 u is an NN32")
    assert((u + 1) = unsigned(6), "u + 1 for an NN32 5 is 6")
    assert(round(2.5_10), 2, "round(2.5_10) is 2")
    assert(round(3.5_10), 4, "round(3.5_10) is 4")

    (* Each number type's = with a numeral, by the pair that goes with its coercion. *)
    u0: NN32 = 0
    assert(u0 = 0, "u = 0 for an NN32 zero")
    v0: NN64 = 0
    assert(v0 = 0, "v = 0 for an NN64 zero")
    f0: RR32 = 0
    assert(f0 = 0, "r = 0 for an RR32 zero")
    assert(f0 = 0.0, "r = 0.0 for an RR32 zero")
    assert(0 = u0, "0 = u for an NN32 zero")
    assert(0.5 = narrow(w), "0.5 = r for an RR32 0.5")
    println "PASS"

content.content:
(* A program's own type receives a numeral through its coercion from the numeral type, which reads the numeral's four numbers, one object per site. *)
component NumeralOwnTypeWalk
export Executable

value object CC64(re: RR64, im: RR64)
    coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) = CC64(asFloat(x), 0.0)
    coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = CC64(asFloat(x), 0.0)
    opr +(self, other: CC64): CC64 = CC64(re + other.re, im + other.im)
    opr juxtaposition(self, other: CC64): CC64 =
        CC64(re other.re - im other.im, re other.im + im other.re)
end

imaginary: CC64 = CC64(0.0, 1.0)

(* The exact rational of a positive normal double. *)
exact(d: RR64): QQ = do
    bits: ZZ64 = d.rawBits
    e: ZZ64 = (bits RSHIFT 52) BITAND 2047
    f: ZZ64 = bits BITAND 4503599627370495
    mant: ZZ = big(f + 4503599627370496)
    k: ZZ32 = (e - 1075).asZZ32
    two: ZZ = big(2)
    if k >= 0 then (mant two^k) / big(1) else mant / two^(-k) end
  end

value object Iv(lo: RR64, hi: RR64)
    coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = do
        q: QQ = x
        d: RR64 = asFloat(x)
        a: QQ = exact(d)
        if a = q then Iv(d, d) elif q < a then Iv(d.nextDown, d) else Iv(d, d.nextUp) end
      end
end

(* bfloat16 for values in [1, 2): sign 0, exponent 127, seven fraction bits, rounded half to even once. *)
value object BF16(bits: ZZ32)
    coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = do
        q: QQ = x
        half: QQ = 1/2
        s: QQ = q (128/1)
        n: ZZ = floor(s)
        rest: QQ = s - (n/1)
        up: Boolean = if rest > half then true elif rest < half then false else odd(n) end
        k: ZZ = if up then n + 1 else n end
        BF16((k - 128 + 16256).asZZ32)
      end
end

value object Dec(unscaled: ZZ, scale: ZZ32)
    coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = Dec(x.digitValue, x.fractionDigits)
end

value object Written(text: String)
    coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = Written(x.asString)
end

object Ref(v: ZZ)
    coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) = Ref(x.digitValue)
end

made(): Ref = 7

parts(x: RadixPointNumeral): String =
    x.digits.asString || " " || x.fractionDigits.asString || " " || x.radix.asString || " " || x.digitValue.asString

same(a: RadixPointNumeral, b: RadixPointNumeral): Boolean = a SEQV b
equal(a: RadixPointNumeral, b: RadixPointNumeral): Boolean = a = b

run(): () = do
    c: CC64 = 3 + 4 imaginary
    assert(c.re SEQV 3.0, "3 + 4 i has the real part 3.0")
    assert(c.im SEQV 4.0, "3 + 4 i has the imaginary part 4.0")
    d: CC64 = 3.78 + 3.243 imaginary
    assert(d.re SEQV 3.78, "3.78 + 3.243 i has the real part 3.78")
    assert(d.im SEQV 3.243, "3.78 + 3.243 i has the imaginary part 3.243")
    assert(parts(3.78), "3 2 10 378", "3.78 has three digits, two after the point, radix 10, value 378")
    assert(parts(3.243), "4 3 10 3243", "3.243 has four digits, three after the point, radix 10, value 3243")
    i1: Iv = 0.1
    assert(i1.lo SEQV 0.09999999999999999, "Iv(0.1) has the double below 1/10 as its low bound")
    assert(i1.hi SEQV 0.1, "Iv(0.1) has the double above 1/10 as its high bound")
    i2: Iv = 0.5
    assert(i2.lo SEQV 0.5, "Iv(0.5) is the point 0.5")
    assert(i2.hi SEQV 0.5, "Iv(0.5) is the point 0.5")
    b: BF16 = 1.00390625000000000001
    assert(b.bits, 16257, "BF16(1.00390625000000000001) rounds once, to 0x3F81")
    b0: BF16 = 1.00390625
    assert(b0.bits, 16256, "BF16(1.00390625), the midpoint, rounds to even, 0x3F80")
    p: Dec = 3.14159
    assert(p.unscaled, big(314159), "Dec(3.14159) has the unscaled value 314159")
    assert(p.scale, 5, "Dec(3.14159) has the scale 5")
    p0: Dec = 3.14150
    assert(p0.unscaled, big(314150), "Dec(3.14150) keeps the unscaled value 314150")
    assert(p0.scale, 5, "Dec(3.14150) keeps the scale 5")
    h: Written = C.8_16
    assert(h.text, "C.8_16", "C.8_16 is written back as C.8_16")
    assert(made() SEQV made(), "one site gives one object of a reference type")
    r1: Ref = 7
    r2: Ref = 7
    assert(NOT (r1 SEQV r2), "two sites give two objects of a reference type")
    assert(same(2.5, 2.50), "2.5 SEQV 2.50 between two numeral values")
    assert(same(0.1_2, 0.5), "0.1_2 SEQV 0.5 between two numeral values")
    assert(NOT equal(0.1, 0.1_16), "0.1 = 0.1_16 is false between two numeral values")
    println "PASS"
  end

end

content.content:
#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table holds a total; 1 if no table could be produced, or if the table holds
# no total because the run's errors are not the checker's (#stopped, below). 20 s in the
# main tree, measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The run stops after the type checker (WorldFlip -stop check), since 2026-10-24 (climb batch
# 22): the compiler's own phase order up to and including TYPECHECK, integer literal folding
# included, as the distance stage's DistanceMulti -order check. Past the checker, the code
# generator's refusals are not the checker's errors (FACTS F-34 counts them), and its first
# one throws, so a run on a library the checker passes went on into the code generator and
# printed no total. A run the checker stops runs the same phases as before; a clean check,
# a run that reached the component's check and ended rc 0 with no error line, reads as 0.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file; its -stop check added 2026-10-24) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
#
# The table, tab-separated, every row tagged:
#   #api        one row per api the checker checked, with that api's error count
#   #total      the errors that the run's last "File X has N errors." line counts, or 0 for
#               a clean check (above)
#   #locations  the distinct file:line those errors were reported at
#   #stopped    in place of #total and #locations, when that line counts errors that the
#               checker did not report: no api's check reported an error and the checker
#               never reached the component, so the library stopped at parse or name
#               binding, before the apis' check or between it and the component's. It names
#               the target, that line and the files the errors were reported in. The gate's
#               checker_compare reads a table with no #total row as NO TOTAL, red.
#   #crash      the first OverloadingChecker crash the checker survived, or none
#   #cache      whether the overloading checker's memo is on (it is off: above)
#   #shadow     whether the instrumented copy still matches the tracked StaticChecker
# test_run.py beside this script tests these readings on canned run outputs.
set -u

STOCK_SHA=16e6e11df9341a67038b7d7cc9f0d7bb5e5a6149019f09e92545a8b646363a0b   # ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java, 2026-09-22

OUT=${1:-}
if [ -z "$OUT" ] ; then echo "usage: $0 <out-file> [scratch-dir]" >&2 ; exit 1 ; fi
case "$OUT" in /*) ;; *) OUT="$PWD/$OUT" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count"
TARGET=Library/FortressLibrary.fss
SCRATCH=${2:-${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/checker-count.$$}
STOCK=$FH/ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java
OVERLOAD_CACHE=false     # the overloading checker's memo, off: see the header

=== XXXNumeralLeftOfRR32Walk.fss
(* A float numeral to the left of an RR32 operand converts into RR32, as it does to the right: RR32's + and juxtaposition are the most specific. *)
component XXXNumeralLeftOfRR32Walk
export Executable

shownV(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    RR32 => v.asString || " : RR32"
    RR64 => v.asString || " : RR64"
    else => v.asString || " : another type"
  end

run(): () = do
    a: RR32 = narrow(1.5)
    assert(shownV(2.5 + a), "4.0 : RR32", "literals.tex, section \"Literals\", and conversions-coercions.tex, section \"Coercion Resolution\": a float numeral + RR32 by RR32's +, the numeral converting into RR32")
    assert(shownV(2.5 a), "3.75 : RR32", "literals.tex, section \"Literals\", and conversions-coercions.tex, section \"Coercion Resolution\": a float numeral juxtaposed with an RR32 by RR32's juxtaposition, the numeral converting into RR32")
    println "PASS"
  end

end

(* ZZ32's big answers exactly at the ends of ZZ32. *)
component ZZ32BigEndsWalk
export Executable

shown(v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    ZZ32 => v.asString || " : ZZ32"
    ZZ64 => v.asString || " : ZZ64"
    NN32 => v.asString || " : NN32"
    NN64 => v.asString || " : NN64"
    ZZ => v.asString || " : ZZ"
    else => v.asString || " : another type"
  end

run(): () = do
    hi: ZZ32 = 2147483647
    lo: ZZ32 = -2147483647 - 1
    assert(shown(big(hi)), "2147483647 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": big of the ZZ32 2^31-1 is exact")
    assert(shown(big(lo)), "-2147483648 : ZZ", "basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\": big of the ZZ32 -2^31 is exact")
    println "PASS"
  end

end

content.content:
Numerals may be either \emph{simple} or \emph{compound}
(as described in \secref{numerals}).

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}

\section{Typecase Expressions}
\seclabel{typecase}

\note{This section should be revised according to the changes in the pattern matching proposal.}

\note{Do we want to support \EXP{\KWD{typecase} \mathord{\KWD{self}} \KWD{of} \ldots}?

How about \EXP{\KWD{typecase} (x, \KWD{self}, y) \KWD{of} \ldots}?

[07/23/2007] \EXP{\mathord{\KWD{self}}} is not allowed in a shorthand form of
\KWD{typecase} expresiosn.
% foo(x) = 8
% bar(x) = 3
% trait Parent
%    foo(x) = 10
%    baz(x) =
%      typecase self of
%        Child => bar(x)
%        Parent => 23
%      end
% end
% trait Child extends Parent
%    bar(x) = foo(x)
% end
\begin{Fortress}
{\tt~}\pushtabs\=\+\( \VAR{foo}(x) = 8\)\\
\( \VAR{bar}(x) = 3\)\\
\( \KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Parent}\)\\
{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{foo}(x) = 10\)\\
\(    \VAR{baz}(x) =\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(      \KWD{typecase} \mathord{\KWD{self}} \KWD{of}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(        \TYP{Child} \Rightarrow \VAR{bar}(x)\)\\
\(        \TYP{Parent} \Rightarrow 23\)\-\\\poptabs
\(      \KWD{end}\)\-\-\\\poptabs\poptabs
\( \KWD{end}\)\\
\( \KWD{trait}\:\TYP{Child} \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{Parent}\)\\
{\tt~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{bar}(x) = \VAR{foo}(x)\)\-\\\poptabs
\( \KWD{end}\)\-\\\poptabs
\end{Fortress}
}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{DelimitedExpr}
&::=& \KWD{typecase} \emph{TypecaseBindings} \KWD{of}
\emph{TypecaseClauses} \option{\emph{CaseElse}} \KWD{end}\\

\emph{TypecaseBindings} &::=& \emph{TypecaseVars}
\options{\EXP{=} \emph{Expr}}\\

\emph{TypecaseVars} &::=& \emph{BindId} \\
&$|$& \texttt{(} \emph{BindId}(\EXP{,} \emph{BindId})$^+$ \texttt{)} \\

\emph{TypecaseClauses} &::=& \emph{TypecaseClause}$^+$\\

\emph{TypecaseClause} &::=&
\emph{TypecaseTypes} \EXP{\Rightarrow} \emph{BlockElems} \\

\emph{TypecaseTypes}
&::=& \texttt{(} \emph{TypeList} \texttt{)}\\
&$|$& \emph{Type} \\

\emph{CaseElse} &::=& \KWD{else} \EXP{\Rightarrow} \emph{BlockElems}\\

\end{Grammar}

A \KWD{typecase} expression begins with \KWD{typecase} followed by
an identifier or a sequence of parenthesized identifiers,
optionally followed by the token \EXP{=} and a \emph{binding} expression,
followed by \KWD{of}, a sequence of typecase clauses
(each consisting of a sequence of \emph{guarding types}
followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow}, followed by an expression block),
an optional \KWD{else} clause
(consisting of \KWD{else} followed by the token \EXP{\Rightarrow},
followed by an expression block),
and finally \KWD{end}.

A \KWD{typecase} expression with a binding expression
evaluates the expression first;
if it completes normally, the value of the expression is bound

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

content.content:
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
coercion from it.
\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
that \library\ give a numeral.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.}

(* A program's generic type receives a numeral through its coercion from the numeral type, at each instance. *)
component NumeralGenericOwnTypeWalk
export Executable

value object Tagged[\T\](v: ZZ, point: Boolean)
    coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) = Tagged[\T\](x.digitValue, false)
    coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = Tagged[\T\](x.digitValue, true)
end

run(): () = do
    a: Tagged[\String\] = 5
    assert(a.v, big(5), "Tagged[\\String\\] receives 5 through its coercion from NaturalNumeral")
    assert(NOT a.point, "5 reaches the coercion from NaturalNumeral")
    b: Tagged[\ZZ32\] = 2.25
    assert(b.v, big(225), "Tagged[\\ZZ32\\] receives 2.25 through its coercion from RadixPointNumeral")
    assert(b.point, "2.25 reaches the coercion from RadixPointNumeral")
    println "PASS"
  end

end

(* A numeral at a declared return type converts through that type's coercion, which may raise. *)
component NumeralAtReturnWalk
export Executable

object Digit(d: ZZ)
    coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) =
        if x.digitValue > big(9) then throw FailCalled("not a digit") else Digit(x.digitValue) end
end

half(): QQ = 0.5
seven(): Digit = 7
twelve(): Digit = 12

raisesFail(f: () -> Any): Boolean =
    try
        f()
        false
    catch e
        FailCalled => true
    end

run(): () = do
    assert(numerator(half()), 1, "half(): QQ = 0.5 answers 1/2")
    assert(denominator(half()), 2, "half(): QQ = 0.5 answers 1/2")
    assert(seven().d, big(7), "seven(): Digit = 7 answers Digit(7)")
    assert(raisesFail(fn () => twelve()), "twelve(): Digit = 12 raises the coercion's FailCalled")
    println "PASS"
  end

end
EOF

Skeptic's fix: a radix-point numeral whose digits after the point are all 0 keeps its radix and its four numbers as written

Walk took the numeral's radix from the node, whose base the parser sets to 1 where every digit after
the point is 0 (nodes_util/ExprFactory.java, makeFloatLiteralExpr), and the written digits did not
parse in radix 1, so 3.0's numeral object was RadixPointNumeral(2, 0, 1, 3), 1.00_16's (3, 0, 1, 1),
and asString of 2.0's looped for ever (numeralDigits divides by its radix 1). The radix now comes from
the numeral's text, as for an integer numeral, and a radix-12 numeral's letters X and E read as the
parser reads them, so 3.0 is (2, 1, 10, 30) and 2.0 writes back as "2.0": the Working Draft's four
numbers (Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex, "Literals"; P-174).

keys to calls that choose differently, and by the rule for reuse, "If any answer differs, the reuse
is wrong" (fortress-repo, compiler.md, "The checker's time"), which a cache of walk's keeps alike.

So parts(3.0) printed 'Zero1 parts(3.0) 2 0 1 3' where the Draft's four numbers are 2 1 10 30, and asString of 2.0's numeral object looped until killed ('Terminated', rc=124).

Defect B (fixed, 794f7d908e): Numerals.inRange looked NN32 up among FortressLibrary's root types, so the NN32 range check never applied. n: NN32 = 5000000000 raised 'IntegerOverflow' from asNN32 instead of the binding's refusal. With h declared at NN32 and at QQ, h(5000000000) raised IntegerOverflow; the same call at ZZ32 answers QQ.

Defect B2 (fixed, 6408011e9b): the dispatch caches' key (Numerals.keys) left out whether NN32 holds a numeral with a ZZ64 default, or NN64 one with a ZZ default. The five defects I measured and fixed, each with a test seen failing first: (A) a radix-point numeral whose digits after the point are all zero got radix 1, so 3.0 read (2, 0, 1, 3) and asString of 2.0's numeral object never returned; (B) NN32's range check never applied, because NN32 is FortressBuiltin's type, so the NN32 coercion ran and raised IntegerOverflow; (B2) the dispatch caches reused an NN32 or NN64 choice for a later numeral outside that range; (C) a program's generic type got no numerals through its coercion from the numeral type; (D, contested) at a declared return type, a numeral that does not convert was returned as its default, and the program's coercion's exception was swallowed. After the last fix, ant testSystem ran 803 tests with one failure, TupleOrderMixedRefused, which is rung G's. Defect A (fixed, e3f9f07dfb): Numerals.radixPoint took its radix from the node, and ExprFactory.makeFloatLiteralExpr sets that base to 1 when every digit after the point is 0. So parts(3.0) printed 'Zero1 parts(3.0) 2 0 1 3' where the Draft's four numbers are 2 1 10 30, and asString of 2.0's numeral object looped until killed ('Terminated', rc=124).

Defect B (fixed, 794f7d908e): Numerals.inRange looked NN32 up among FortressLibrary's root types, so the NN32 range check never applied. n: NN32 = 5000000000 raised 'IntegerOverflow' from asNN32 instead of the binding's refusal. With h declared at NN32 and at QQ, h(5000000000) raised IntegerOverflow; the same call at ZZ32 answers QQ.

Defect B2 (fixed, 6408011e9b): the dispatch caches' key (Numerals.keys) left out whether NN32 holds a numeral with a ZZ64 default, or NN64 one with a ZZ default. After the fix for B, 'Cache5 h(3000000000) NN32' followed by h(5000000000) raised 'IntegerOverflow'; the same call made fresh answers 'Cache6 h(5000000000) QQ'.

Defect C (fixed, 43d019ed3b): Coercions.numeralCoercionFor ignored the coercions of a program's generic type. g: GBox[\String\] = 5 was refused with 'RHS expression type Int is not assignable to LHS type GBox[\String\]', although genericCoercionFor finds that type's coercion from any other value.

Defect D (fixed, contested, 953d050966): Numerals.atReturn returned a numeral's default when the declared return type could not take it, and caught every FortressException. big32(): ZZ32 = 3000000000 returned 'Ret1 ZZ64 3000000000'; mk(): OnlyZ = 3 returned 'Ret3 ZZ32 3'; mk(): Picky = 12 returned 'Ret4 ZZ32 12', where the binding raises 'FailCalled'.

Numerals are stored as their defaults: a value read back from Box(0.5).v, a typecase binding, an array element, Just(0.5).get or a declared RR64 result is refused at a QQ parameter, as on the old code. A numeral that flows through an if-expression is still a numeral at the parameter ('Leak3 NN32 5'). Today's checker gives such an if the branches' type NaturalNumeral (Misc.scala:526-575), so the two agree; a note for rung C, whose join rule may differ.
